abstract: "Mental rotation — the ability to mentally transform an object’s orientation in space — is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive psychology, yet evidence for its cross-cultural validity in children remains limited. We examined performance on the LEVANTE (Learning Variability Network Exchange) mental rotation task across four international study sites in three countries (Colombia, Germany, and Canada) for 1,037 children aged 5–13 years (411 girls, 427 boys, 199 unknown). Item parameters were shared across sites, with models constraining discriminations strongly preferred over a configural model (2PL scalar invariance model; ΔBIC = 417 vs. configural invariance model). The angular disparity effect (Shepard and Metzler, 1971) replicated for both 2D and 3D stimuli ($\\beta$ = 0.16, SE = 0.004, p < .001), with response times being approximately 16.9% slower per 40° of stimulus rotation angle. Mental rotation abilities increased with age ($\\beta$ = 0.33, SE = 0.02, p < .001) and did not differ by sex ($\\beta$ = -0.00, SE = 0.08, p = .998). Boys responded 7.4% faster than girls ($\\beta$ = -0.08, SE = 0.03, p = .004). These findings establish that the task captures a consistent, spatially-driven construct across culturally diverse samples — a necessary precondition for using cross-cultural data to understand variation in spatial reasoning. "

impact-statement: "Mental rotation is the ability to imagine turning an object in your mind. We tested this skill in 1,037 children aged 5–13 in Colombia, Germany and Canada. The test measured the same underlying skill across all four study sites, supporting its use to compare children across these settings. Boys answered somewhat faster than girls, but were no more accurate. Children took longer to respond when objects needed more mental turning, whether the shapes were two-dimensional or three-dimensional. Performance improved with age, and we found no difference in accuracy between boys and girls. These findings provide a foundation for studying how spatial thinking develops and varies across different cultural settings."

From fitting puzzle pieces together at age three to navigating complex diagrams in school, spatial reasoning underpins a broad array of cognitive achievements — and children differ substantially as individuals in how these skills develop.
Such variability is detectable early, across a wide range of spatial tasks in primary school-aged children [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and its consequences are far-reaching: spatial ability predicts outcomes spanning creative domains such as music [@padulo2020effects; @hetland2000learning] and the visual arts [@kell2013creativity; @winner2013relationship], mathematical achievement [@gunderson2012relation], science learning [@gilligan2020first], and long-term educational and occupational outcomes in STEM fields [@wai2009spatial]. Understanding what drives this variability is therefore a question of both theoretical and practical importance. The present study takes a step toward that goal by examining children's performance on a mental rotation task across four international study sites, asking both what is consistent across cultures and what varies.

Spatial reasoning encompasses abilities for representing, transforming, and reasoning about visuospatial information [@lohman1996spatial]. Rather than a single unified capacity, it is better understood as a family of related but distinguishable skills, including mental rotation, spatial visualization, perspective-taking, and navigation, that differ in the type of spatial information involved and the cognitive operations required [@uttal2013malleability; @newcombe2018three]. These skills can be organized along two dimensions: whether the spatial relations are intrinsic to an object or extrinsic between objects, and whether the task requires dynamic mental transformation or only static representation [@uttal2013malleability]. Mental rotation — the focus of the present study — falls in the intrinsic-dynamic quadrant of this framework, involving the mental transformation of a single object's orientation in space.

The classic mental rotation task, first developed by @shepard1971mental, presents participants with pairs of objects at varying angular disparities and asks them to judge whether the objects are identical or mirror-reversed, with response time and accuracy as the key dependent variables. It is one of the most studied spatial skills in cognitive psychology. The dominant account of how people solve it — 'pure' or analog rotation — holds that the solver constructs a holistic mental image of the object and continuously rotates it until it aligns with the target. Because the mental image must traverse each intermediate angle, larger rotations take proportionally longer [@shepard1971mental; @cooper1973chronometric]. The result is one of the most robust and replicable findings in the field: response times increase approximately linearly with angular disparity (i.e., how far an object has been rotated from its original orientation).

The original paradigm used 3D block figures, and adult research has predominantly followed suit. Developmental research, however, has tended to use simpler 2D stimuli — animal silhouettes or abstract shapes — on the grounds that 3D figures may be too demanding for younger children [@jansen2013mental], and studies of spatial development in middle childhood have mainly relied on 2D stimuli [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. As a result, the adult and child literatures have largely developed in parallel, and whether the angular disparity effect holds comparably for 2D and 3D stimuli across the primary school years remains poorly understood. 
<!-- The LEVANTE task offers an opportunity to examine this directly, as it includes both stimulus types within the same paradigm across a broad developmental window.  -->


Mental rotation ability develops across a prolonged period from infancy through adolescence. Precursors of successful rotation are detectable in the first year of life [@frick2014development; @moore2008mental], and performance on explicit rotation tasks improves substantially across the preschool years [@frick2013development] and continues to develop through middle childhood [@marmor1975development; @kail1980developmental], with further refinement into adolescence. This extended developmental trajectory makes the primary school years, ages 5--13 years, a particularly informative window for studying how mental rotation skills are acquired and how they vary across children.

Some variation in mental rotation ability may be related to individuals' sex.^[We refer to sex differences throughout (in the sense of the biological variable), though some observed differences may reflect gender-related factors such as socialization and experience. We remain agnostic about this question here.] Sex differences in mental rotation are well documented in adults [@voyer1995magnitude; @zell2015evaluating], but in children the picture is considerably less clear. @lauer2019development synthesized data from over 30,000 children aged 3--17, finding no reliable sex difference in the preschool years, a small male advantage emerging around age 6 (g $\approx$ 0.20), and a moderate effect only by age 14, with task and stimulus characteristics explaining substantial variability independently of age. This sensitivity to stimulus type and age has been documented most systematically in German primary school children. The gap is typically absent in younger children and emerges around age 10, concentrated in more demanding cube figure conditions — particularly for girls, who show less improvement across grades than boys [@neuburger2011gender; @jansen2013mental]. However, the direction of the difference can reverse entirely under female-congruent stimulus conditions [@ruthsatz2017gender; @ruthsatz2019girls]. Evidence from other countries is similarly inconsistent: male advantages have been reported in Italian children from age 8 [@moe2018mental], in Dutch children aged 7–9 though not in older children in the same sample [@van2019sex], and in French children at age 11–12 but not at 7–8 [@hoyek2011use]. In contrast, no significant sex difference was found across the full primary school age range in a UK sample [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. Whether these discrepancies reflect genuine cultural variation, differences in task format, or both remains unclear.

Finally, the vast majority of developmental research on mental rotation has been conducted with children in middle-to-high-income Western convenience populations [@henrich2010weirdest], raising questions about whether findings about its developmental trajectory, psychometric properties, and underlying cognitive processes generalize beyond the populations in which they were established. The limited cross-cultural evidence that does exist spans different populations, developmental periods, and spatial tasks, making it difficult to draw firm conclusions about how cultural context shapes performance. Studies with children from two small-scale societies — including Tsimané forager-horticulturalists in Bolivia [@davis2019spatial] and seminomadic pastoralist-forager children in northern Namibia [@davis2021cultural] — successfully adapted mental rotation for these populations but did not make comparisons between populations. In one of the few studies to examine mental rotation cross-culturally in children, researchers compared children in the Ivory Coast and Switzerland and found that the overall shape of the RT–angle curve was similar across both groups, suggesting the basic mental rotation signature is present in both cultural contexts [@nunez1998mental]. However, age predicted performance in the Swiss group but not the Ivorian group, pointing to the possibility that the developmental trajectory of mental rotation differs across cultures even when its basic signature holds. Yet the study has important limitations — it was small (n = 151) and relied on a computerized task likely more familiar to Swiss children. Notably, the authors themselves attributed much of the observed RT difference to cultural differences in familiarity with technology and the value placed on speed, rather than to differences in spatial cognition per se. Taken together, the cross-cultural validity of the mental rotation paradigm with children remains largely unestablished.

In sum, a review of the existing work on mental rotation suggests three gaps. First, we have limited data on whether mental rotation tasks developed and validated in well-resourced contexts measure the same underlying construct when administered to children from different cultural and socioeconomic backgrounds. Second, even where cross-cultural comparisons have been made, they have rarely examined whether performance shows the same characteristic patterns across contexts. The linear relationship between response time and angular disparity has been demonstrated repeatedly in middle-to-high-income Western samples of children and adults [@kaltner2016developmental; @jansen2015role], but its replicability across varied international contexts remains largely untested. Third, whether and when sex differences in mental rotation emerge in primary school children remains unclear, with findings varying substantially across studies and tasks — making it a natural question to examine in a cross-cultural dataset. We address these gaps with three sets of corresponding analyses, each building toward a broader understanding of how and why children's spatial reasoning varies across cultures.

## Present study

The present study uses data from the Learning Variability Network Exchange (LEVANTE), an international research collaboration designed to capture how children's learning and development vary across ages and cultural contexts. LEVANTE's central aim is to build a large, openly shared dataset of children's cognitive development across diverse settings, with a particular focus on individual variability — what differs across children, and why. Data were collected by three research teams from four geographically and culturally diverse pilot sites: the Universidad de los Andes in Bogotá, Colombia (uniandes-co-bogota) and nearby rural areas (uniandes-co-rural); the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany (mpieva-de); and the University of Western Ontario in London, Canada (western-ca). Here we use data from a single task in the LEVANTE battery: a mental rotation task designed and scored using an item response theory measurement approach, which allows directly comparable ability estimates to be derived across children who completed different subsets of items [@Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks]. 

Our goal is not to compare absolute levels of performance. Indeed, LEVANTE is not designed to support site-level performance comparisons — sites vary substantially in sampling, recruitment, and test administration in ways that heavily confound absolute comparisons. Differences in overall scores across sites should therefore not be interpreted as reflecting population differences. However, examining the consistency of patterns within each site can still be informative about both measurement and theoretical questions; hence, this is the approach we take here.

Our first research question asks whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task achieves measurement invariance across international study sites — that is, whether the task captures the same underlying construct regardless of where it is administered. Our second asks whether response time performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli, as originally demonstrated by @shepard1971mental, using the angular disparity effect as the key benchmark: as the angular difference between two objects increases, so too should the time required to judge whether they match. If children across four culturally diverse sites show this same systematic pattern, this constitutes good evidence that the task is engaging the spatial demands it was designed to capture. Our third research question examines age and sex differences in mental rotation ability, including their interaction, and sex differences in response time. These three questions move from psychometric structure (cross-site invariance), to process-level validity (angular sensitivity), to individual variation (demographic differences), building a layered case for the task's cross-cultural validity.

# Methods

## Participants

Data were drawn from four LEVANTE pilot sites administered by three partner teams: at Universidad de los Andes administered in Bogotá, Colombia (uniandes-co-bogota) and nearby rural areas (uniandes-co-rural); at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology administered in Leipzig, Germany (mpieva-de); and at the University of Western Ontario administered in London, Ontario, Canada (western-ca). Site codes rather than country names are used throughout to reflect that each site represents data collected by a single institution from one or several distinct samples within a large, diverse country, and should not be taken as representative of national populations.

### Colombia
The Universidad de los Andes sites (uniandes-co-bogota and uniandes-co-rural) recruited children aged 5--13 years across six schools in Colombia: four in Bogotá — three affiliated with family compensation funds and one managed by a charter school organisation — and two public schools in the rural departments of Caquetá (i.e., in a municipality located northeast of Florencia) and Boyacá (i.e., in a municipality close to Chiquinquira). Bogotá is the largest and most populous city in Colombia, with a population of over seven million individuals residing within the urban area [@statsco], and substantial variation in socioeconomic status [@statsco]. Florencia and Chiquinquira are smaller municipalities with populations of over 150,000 individuals and 50,000 individuals respectively [@statsco]. Children were recruited from schools with existing partnerships with the Universidad de los Andes. Children completed the tasks individually using tablets. A researcher supervised groups of children completing the tasks simultaneously, with group size altered for the age of the children (smaller groups for younger children). For uniandes-co-bogota, data for the mental rotation task were collected from `{r} site_spans[["uniandes-co-bogota"]]$earliest` to `r site_spans[["uniandes-co-bogota"]]$latest` and are comprised of `{r} site_n[["uniandes-co-bogota"]]$n_runs` assessments from `{r} site_n[["uniandes-co-bogota"]]$n_users` participants; for uniandes-co-rural they were collected from `{r} site_spans[["uniandes-co-rural"]]$earliest` to `r site_spans[["uniandes-co-rural"]]$latest` and are comprised of `{r} site_n[["uniandes-co-rural"]]$n_runs` assessments from `{r} site_n[["uniandes-co-rural"]]$n_users` participants.

### Germany
The Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology site (mpieva-de) collected data from children aged 5--13 years in Leipzig, Germany. Leipzig is a mid-sized urban centre with a population of approximately 600,000 individuals [@statsde], and participants in the current study mainly came from middle- to upper-middle-income backgrounds. Children and their families were recruited from an existing database of Leipzig residents via telephone and completed tasks remotely at home using their own devices. Data for the mental rotation task were collected from `{r} site_spans[["mpieva-de"]]$earliest` to `r site_spans[["mpieva-de"]]$latest` and are comprised of `{r} site_n[["mpieva-de"]]$n_runs` assessments from `{r} site_n[["mpieva-de"]]$n_users` participants.

### Canada
The Western University site (western-ca) recruited children aged 5--13 years primarily from London, Ontario, with a smaller number from the Greater Toronto Area. London is a medium-sized urban and suburban area with a population of over 400,000 individuals [@statscan]. The Greater Toronto Area is a large urban and suburban area, comprising the city of Toronto and four surrounding regional municipalities, and is the most population metropolitan region in Canada with a population of over 6 million individuals [@statscan]. Canadian participants in the current study mainly came from middle- to upper-middle-income backgrounds. Recruitment relied on online outreach through social media and community groups, supplemented by local posters and school newsletters. Children were assessed individually by a researcher in a dedicated campus testing space. Data for the mental rotation task were collected from `{r} site_spans[["western-ca"]]$earliest` to `r site_spans[["western-ca"]]$latest` and are comprised of `{r} site_n[["western-ca"]]$n_runs` assessments from `{r} site_n[["western-ca"]]$n_users` participants.

Site-level sampling characteristics are described in @tbl-participants-qualitative and @tbl-participants-quantitative. Due to de-identification protocols, individual-level demographic data — including socioeconomic indicators — are not available for the current sample. `r n_excluded$n_runs` assessments were excluded, comprising `r excl_str`. `r n_final$n_users` of the `r n_assessed_users` children assessed contributed at least one retained assessment (`r overall_sex_counts$Female` female, `r overall_sex_counts$Male` male, `r overall_sex_counts$Unknown` unknown), giving a final sample of n = `r n_final$n_runs` assessments. `r n_repeat_users` of these children contributed two retained assessments each; each assessment was treated as a separate observation, with participant included as a random effect in all mixed-effects models to account for the non-independence between a child's assessments. 

## Ethics approval

Each participating site is responsible for obtaining ethical approval for its own data collection from the relevant institutional and/or governmental ethics committees, and for obtaining informed consent in accordance with local regulations and institutional guidelines. Only fully de-identified data are contributed to the LEVANTE Data Repository (LDR); the analyses reported here draw exclusively on such data, and participant identities cannot be readily ascertained or otherwise associated with the data by LDR staff or secondary data users.

## Measure

The nine core tasks in the LEVANTE battery, including mental rotation, were initially designed in English and then subsequently adapted for Spanish and German following a set of internationalization procedures in collaboration with researchers at the uniandes-co and mpieva-de sites, respectively. The LEVANTE mental rotation task [originally based on @frick2013development] is administered digitally on a tablet or computer as part of a battery of nine core tasks. In the version analyzed here, it employs two stimulus categories of increasing difficulty: 2D animal figures (ducks and rabbits), and 3D block configurations from the @shepard1971mental set (Figure S1); subsequent versions available through the LEVANTE website add a small number of other stimuli. On each trial, a target image is displayed alongside two alternatives: one shows the same object rotated to a different angle, and the other is a mirror-reversed version that cannot be matched to the target by rotation alone. Children select whichever alternative they judge to correspond to the target by tapping or clicking on their device. The angular disparity between target and correct alternative varies systematically across trials (ranging from 20° to 320°), enabling examination of how increasing rotation demands affect both accuracy and response latency.

<!-- ### Computer-adaptive testing format -->

The mental rotation task was released in a computer-adaptive testing (CAT) format midway through the pilot data collection period. In the adaptive version, participant ability is summarized by a latent proficiency estimate ($\theta$) that is re-estimated after each response. The updated $\theta$ then guides selection of the next item so that it is appropriately challenging for each individual child. This trial-by-trial targeting typically makes the task more engaging and increases measurement efficiency, enabling reliable ability estimation with fewer administered items. In the present sample, `r cat_counts$runs$pct_cat`% of administrations (`r cat_counts$runs$n_cat` of `r cat_counts$runs$n_total`) used the CAT format. In the fixed format, testing stopped after either six consecutive incorrect responses or a maximum of 10 minutes, whichever came first. See @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks for more information on the internationalization procedures and CAT versions of all LEVANTE tasks.

## Analysis

<!-- ### Item screening -->
<!-- Prior to fitting psychometric models, we examined item-level performance within each site to identify poorly functioning items. Items were screened for having average accuracy near or below chance, low item–total correlations, high missingness, or other anomalous patterns – as a result no items were identified as warranting exclusion from further analysis for this task. For full details of the item screening procedure, see @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks. -->

### Data preparation
Trials were excluded from all analyses if they had response times greater than 30s or smaller than 100ms.
Rotation angles were recoded to their shortest-path equivalents, collapsing the full 0–360° range to angular disparities of 0–180° (e.g., a 320° rotation was treated as a 40° disparity), on the assumption that participants take the most efficient rotational path.
This recoding was verified in a robustness check using full 0–360° angles for the 2D stimuli, which were presented in both rotational directions (Figure S6).

### Item response theory models
Item response theory (IRT) is a psychometric framework that models the relationship between a latent trait and performance on individual task items [@embretson2013item]. Unlike classical test theory, which relies on total scores and treats all items as equivalent contributors to measurement, IRT estimates item-level parameters independently of the specific sample tested, providing more precise measurement across the ability range. All models assumed a single underlying factor, following standard practice in psychometric analyses of mental rotation tasks and consistent with the task's design as a measure of a single spatial ability.

We compared two types of IRT models. The Rasch model [@rasch1960probabilistic], or 1-parameter logistic (1PL) model, estimates only item difficulty, holding discrimination constant across items — that is, it assumes all items are equally good at differentiating children of higher versus lower ability. The two-parameter logistic model (2PL) relaxes this constraint, additionally estimating each item's discrimination parameter. A better-fitting 2PL therefore indicates that items vary meaningfully in how well they distinguish between ability levels. For both types of models we additionally fixed the lower asymptote at chance (0.5), rather than estimating it, because items have two response options. Strictly these are therefore a 1PL and a 2PL with a fixed guessing parameter, sometimes written 1PL-G and 2PL-G, rather than the pure forms. We refer to them as Rasch and 2PL throughout for brevity.

All IRT models were estimated in R using the `mirt` package [@chalmers2012mirt] via marginal maximum likelihood with 61 quadrature points. To avoid extreme estimates of difficulty and discrimination in sparse data, we specified a Gaussian prior on item difficulty ($\mathcal{N}(0,3)$) for both Rasch and 2PL models, as well as a Gaussian prior on item discrimination ($\mathcal{N}(1,0.3)$) for 2PL models. We extracted ability scores ($\theta$) using expected a posteriori (EAP) scoring.

### Cross-site invariance
To assess cross-site measurement invariance, we fit both types of models with varying constraints across the four sites: configural invariance (all parameters free to vary), metric invariance (item discriminations are constrained to be equal -- only relevant for 2PL), and scalar invariance (both discriminations and difficulties are constrained to be equal across sites). We compared models using BIC (Bayesian information criterion) as the selection criterion [@putnick2016measurement], and also examined their marginal reliability.

### Angular sensitivity
To investigate whether performance was sensitive to rotation angle as originally demonstrated by @shepard1971mental, we fit linear mixed-effects models (in R using the `lme4` package, @lme4) predicting response time (in log transformed seconds) from angle, stimulus type, site, age, and all of their possible interactions, along with participant-level random intercepts and random slopes of angle. Response times were log transformed to reduce right skew and to stabilise variance across the wide range of baseline speeds in this age range; slopes are therefore multiplicative effects, and are reported as the percentage change in response time per 40° of rotation. Table S5 reports the same effects on the untransformed scale, expressed as rotation rates in degrees per second for comparison with @shepard1971mental, together with the basis for modelling on the log scale.
Children were grouped into three age bands, 5--7, 8--10 and 11--13 years, with each band including children up to but not including their next birthday at the upper bound. Rotation angle was centered and scaled to this unit. Because uniandes-co-rural was administered entirely in adaptive format, the effect of adaptive administration cannot be separated from the effect of site there, and a model containing their interaction is rank deficient. We therefore modelled adaptive administration and its interaction with stimulus type, but not its interaction with either site or angle. Omitting these interactions leaves the estimated angle slopes effectively unchanged. One consequence is that the model does not represent any difference in angular sensitivity between the two formats, so we do not report angle slopes broken down by format. Doing so would describe the differing site composition of the two formats rather than an effect of administration, since adaptive trials are drawn disproportionately from uniandes-co-rural and fixed-form trials not at all. The format check reported below is restricted to the sites that used both formats, where the two can be compared directly.
We used the `performance` package [@performance] to extract model fit statistics and the `marginaleffects` package [@marginaleffects] to extract marginal estimates of angle slopes and other effects of interest. Reported slopes are average marginal effects over the observed trials (see @fig-rt-angle). For comparison with slopes estimated using a balanced grid of cells, see Tables S2 and S3.
Incorrect responses and each run's first trial were excluded from RT analyses. Sample sizes for each site, age group, item type and angle are given in Table S2.

Of `r cat_counts$trials$n_total` trials from all assessments, `r cat_counts$trials$n_cat` (`r cat_counts$trials$pct_cat`%) were administered in computer-adaptive (CAT) format.
These were retained, with administration format modelled as a predictor, rather than excluded. All assessments at uniandes-co-rural were adaptive, so excluding CAT trials would remove that site from the analysis entirely.
Adaptive item selection could in principle bias the estimated angle effect by making angle exposure depend on ability, but three checks suggest it does not do so here.
The run-level association between accuracy and mean angle administered is weaker under adaptive than fixed-form administration (*r* = `r round(cat_angle_sel[["cat"]], 2)` and `r round(cat_angle_sel[["fixed"]], 2)` respectively). The estimated angle slope does not differ significantly between the two formats ($\Delta\beta$ = `r round(cat_slope_diff$estimate, 3)`, SE = `r round(cat_slope_diff$std.error, 3)`, *t* = `r round(cat_slope_diff$statistic, 2)`). Because that comparison pools across sites, and format is confounded with site, we repeated it within the `r cat_within_sites` sites that used both formats, which removes the confound entirely. The slopes again do not differ ($\Delta$ = `r round(cat_slope_diff_within$estimate, 3)`, SE = `r round(cat_slope_diff_within$std.error, 3)`, *p* `r fmt_p(cat_slope_diff_within$p.value)`). 

### Demographic differences
To examine whether IRT-based ability scores differed by age and sex, we fitted a linear mixed-effects model (in R using the `lme4` package) predicting ability scores from sex, age, site, and all of their interactions, with random intercepts for participant.
Site was included as a fixed rather than a random effect given the small number of sites (k = 4), and its interactions with age and sex were retained so that demographic effects could be examined within each site as well as on average.
Sex at birth was reported by caregivers as part of the LEVANTE background survey.
We additionally fit the same angular sensitivity model described above, but with the addition of a sex predictor (in a separate model due to the high rate of missingness of sex). Sex coverage varied across sites: it was complete at uniandes-co-bogota, but unavailable for `r sex_coverage[["uniandes-co-rural"]]$pct_unknown`% of participants at uniandes-co-rural, `r sex_coverage[["mpieva-de"]]$pct_unknown`% at mpieva-de, and `r sex_coverage[["western-ca"]]$pct_unknown`% at western-ca. The sex analyses are therefore based on a sample that is differently composed from the full sample, with Colombian participants comparatively over-represented.
We used the same methods as described above for extracting model performance and estimating marginal effects.


# Results

{{< include _01_irt.qmd >}}
## Cross-site invariance

Our first research question asked whether the task measured the mental rotation construct in the same way across all four sites — that is, whether it achieves measurement invariance. The 2PL scalar invariance model had the lowest BIC (BIC = `r bic_2pl_scalar`), outperforming the 2PL configural invariance model by `r delta_bic_configural` BIC points and the Rasch scalar invariance model by `r delta_bic_rasch` BIC points (see @tbl-mrot-irt). AIC, which penalises parameters less heavily, instead favours the metric model (AIC = `r aic_2pl_metric` against `r aic_2pl_scalar` for scalar), and we return to this below.

The better fit of the 2PL model compared to the Rasch model indicates that mental rotation items vary in their discrimination — specifically, items with higher angular disparity provide more information at higher abilities (Figure S2). Item difficulty and discrimination parameters were broadly similar across sites, with some departures among the 3D items (Figures S3 and S4). Marginal reliabilities are also much higher under the 2PL model (2PL: `r rxx[["2pl"]]`; Rasch: `r rxx$rasch`). This gap should not be read as independent evidence, however, since the Rasch model fixes every discrimination at 1 while the estimated discriminations are considerably larger, and an item with a discrimination of 1 and a floor at chance carries little information. The reliability difference is therefore largely a consequence of the constraint rather than a separate finding.

Both invariance models that constrain discriminations across sites are strongly preferred over the configural model, meaning that items are ordered similarly in difficulty and discriminate similarly wherever they are administered. The stricter scalar model, which additionally constrains difficulties, has the lowest BIC here and would further imply that the absolute spacing between items on the latent scale is preserved across sites.

That last step is less secure than the rest. These are maximum a posteriori fits under a slope prior of N(1, 0.3) shared across all LEVANTE tasks, and because that prior shrinks discriminations toward equality it contributes to the selection among invariance models. Refitting the same five models across a range of slope priors shows that the rejection of configural invariance is robust, holding under every specification we examined, whereas the narrower choice between metric and scalar is not. Scalar is preferred under the N(1, 0.3) and N(1, 0.5) priors and metric under weaker ones, and outside the tightest prior the two are never separated by more than about four BIC points (Table S1). We therefore treat the evidence for shared discriminations as strong and the evidence for the stricter scalar constraint as suggestive rather than settled. Reassuringly, the substantive conclusions reported below do not depend on this choice. Taking $\theta$ from the metric model instead of the scalar model leaves the age effect (0.24 against 0.23 standard deviations per year), the absence of a sex difference, and the absence of an age-by-sex interaction essentially unchanged. What does change is the apparent size of site-level mean differences, which we do not interpret in any case.

Measurement invariance is a psychometric property of the instrument. It establishes that scores can be meaningfully compared across contexts, though it does not license inferences about the causes of any absolute differences, and it does not by itself speak to what cognitive process is driving performance. Evidence that children are engaging the spatial demands the task was designed to capture — specifically, the predicted increase in response time with angular disparity — is addressed in the angular sensitivity analysis below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mrot-irt
#| tbl-cap: "**Model fit indices for IRT models fit to overlapping items.** Overlapping items are those administered at every site, the only set on which a multigroup model can be identified. Note: 2PL = 2-parameter logistic model; Rasch model constrains all item discriminations to be equal. Configural invariance allows all parameters to vary across groups; metric constrains discriminations across groups; scalar constrains discriminations and difficulties. The selected model (bold) had the lowest BIC; ΔBIC indicates the difference in BIC for each model from that minimum. Models are fit by maximum a posteriori estimation under a slope prior of N(1, 0.3) and a difficulty prior of N(0, 3), so the log-posterior rather than the log-likelihood is the quantity maximised; it is reported here for that reason. Because the configural model applies the slope prior separately within each site, it carries more prior terms than the models that constrain discriminations, and its unpenalised log-likelihood is accordingly not comparable with theirs. Table S1 reports the same comparison across a range of slope priors."

mod_tbl |>
  arrange(desc(itemtype), n_pars) |>
  mutate(itemtype = itemtype |> fct_recode("Rasch" = "rasch", "2PL" = "2pl") |>
           as.character()) |>
  select(itemtype, invariance, n_pars, logPost, AIC, BIC, d_BIC) |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(title = md("")) |>
  cols_label(itemtype = "Model",
             invariance = "Invariance",
             n_pars = "Parameters",
             logPost = "Log-posterior",
             d_BIC = "ΔBIC") |>
  tab_style(style = list(cell_text(weight = "bold"),
                         cell_fill(color = "#f0f7ff")),
            locations = cells_body(rows = d_BIC == 0))
```

{{< include _02_angle_sensitivity.qmd >}}
## Angular sensitivity

Our second research question asked whether trial-level performance is sensitive to the spatial properties of the stimuli — specifically, whether the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental replicates across all four sites.
After exclusion of incorrect trials and each run's first trial, a total of `r angle_stats$n_runs` assessments contributed `r angle_stats$n_trials` trials to the analysis (M age = `r angle_stats$age_mean`, SD = `r angle_stats$age_sd`).
Our model predicts response time (in log transformed seconds) from angle (20°--160°), stimulus type (2D duck, 2D rabbit, 3D), site (uniandes-co-bogota, uniandes-co-rural, mpieva-de, western-ca), age (`r angle_stats$age_min`--`r angle_stats$age_max` years), and all of their possible interactions, along with participant-level random intercepts and random slopes of angle.
This model's conditional $r^2$ (i.e. variance explained by both fixed and random effects) was `r mod_stats_tbl$R2_conditional`, its marginal $r^2$ (i.e. variance explained by only fixed effects) was `r mod_stats_tbl$R2_marginal`, and its RMSE (root mean squared error) is `r mod_stats_tbl$RMSE` on the log scale, equivalent to a multiplicative error of about `r mod_stats_tbl$RMSE_exp`× in response time. @fig-rt-angle shows the resulting model fits as a function of angle, along with empirical means and individual data points, stratified by site and age group (age was modeled as continuous and only binned for visualization or marginalization).

Overall there was a strong positive effect of rotation angle, in that the average marginal effect (slope) of angle was `r slope_str(slope("mrot"))`, confirming that response times increased systematically with angular disparity across the full sample.
Since RT is modeled in log space, this corresponds to response times approximately `r slope("mrot")$interpretation` of stimulus rotation.

The two stimulus types differ in overall response time: at the angles both were administered (40--120°), 3D items took `r round(dim_ratio$ratio, 2)`× as long as 2D items ($b$ = `r round(dim_ratio$estimate, 2)`, SE = `r round(dim_ratio$std.error, 3)`, *t* = `r round(dim_ratio$statistic, 1)`).
Their angle slopes cannot be compared over their full ranges, because 3D items were not administered at 160° and the angle function is not linear. Including the 120--160° segment raises the 2D slope from `r round(common_slopes[["2d"]]$estimate, 2)` to `r round(slope("2d")$estimate, 2)`, so over their own ranges the two types appear indistinguishable ($\Delta$ = `r round(full_contrast$estimate, 3)`, *p* `r fmt_p(full_contrast$p.value)`) only because 2D gains a steep segment that 3D never received. Restricted to the angles both types did receive, the slope is slightly steeper for 3D ($\beta$ = `r round(common_slopes[["3d"]]$estimate, 2)`, `r mult_to_pct(exp(common_slopes[["3d"]]$estimate), "slower", "faster")` per `r deg`°) than for 2D ($\beta$ = `r round(common_slopes[["2d"]]$estimate, 2)`, `r mult_to_pct(exp(common_slopes[["2d"]]$estimate), "slower", "faster")` per `r deg`°; $\Delta$ = `r round(common_contrast$estimate, 3)`, SE = `r round(common_contrast$std.error, 3)`, *p* `r fmt_p(common_contrast$p.value)`). These percentages are for the shared `r min(shared_angles)`--`r max(shared_angles)`° range, so they are not directly comparable with the whole-sample figure given above, which covers the full range of angles administered. Both contrasts appear in @tbl-slopes.

The 3D slope is also the estimate most sensitive to how trials are weighted. Averaging over the observed trials gives `r sprintf("%.2f", obs_item_slopes[["3d"]])`, whereas weighting all cells of the design equally gives `r sprintf("%.2f", grid_item_slopes[["3d"]])`; the corresponding 2D estimates are `r sprintf("%.2f", obs_item_slopes[["2d"]])` and `r sprintf("%.2f", grid_item_slopes[["2d"]])` (Table S4). The reason is that 3D items were administered disproportionately to older children, who show the steepest slopes, so averaging over the observed trials weights the 3D estimate toward them. Equal weighting instead leans on cells in which few children received 3D items at all, the sparsest containing fewer than 200 trials. We report observed-trial averaging throughout for that reason, but the angular sensitivity of the 3D items is less precisely pinned down than that of the 2D items. The effect is clearly present under either scheme.

Response time is only one half of the signature reported by @shepard1971mental. If larger rotations demand more processing, accuracy should fall as response time rises, and a model of accuracy therefore provides a check that the response time effect does not simply reflect children becoming more cautious at larger angles. Across the `r acc_stats$n_trials` administered trials from `r acc_stats$n_runs` assessments, accuracy declined by `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(acc_overall$pp))` percentage points per 40° of rotation (SE = `r sprintf("%.1f", acc_overall$pp_se)`, *p* `r acc_overall$p.value`), from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*acc_at("2d", 20))`% at 20° to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100*acc_at("2d", 160))`% at 160° for 2D items. The decline is of comparable size for both stimulus types (2D `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(acc_type("2d")$pp))` points per 40°, 3D `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(acc_type("3d")$pp))` points), and holds within every site and age band (Table S9). Speed and accuracy therefore degrade together as angular disparity grows, which is what continuous rotation predicts and what a shift toward more cautious responding would not produce.

The angle effect was further moderated by site and by age (see @tbl-slopes).
Differences among sites were small but reliable, ranging from `r slope("uniandes-co-rural")$interpretation` at uniandes-co-rural to `r slope("mpieva-de")$interpretation` at mpieva-de.
The age gradient was larger, rising monotonically from `r slope(age_band_labels[1])$interpretation` in 5--7 year olds to `r slope(age_band_labels[3])$interpretation` in 11--13 year olds.

The primary analyses model angle as a linear predictor over the 20–160° range. This is an approximation rather than a claim about the shape of the underlying function, which is not exactly linear, as the steeper 120–160° segment noted above already shows, and @fig-rt-angle suggests further departures within some subgroups. Per-run response times underlying these trends are shown in Figure S5. A separate check using the full 0–360° range bears on a different assumption, that children rotate via the shorter available route so that a 320° rotation behaves like a 40° disparity. The 2D stimuli show the inverted-U about 180° that this predicts, although the recoding holds approximately rather than exactly, with responses just above 180° reliably slower than their mirrored counterparts just below it (Figure S6 and Table S6). The available 3D figures were supplied at only three rotations, all greater than 180°, so the equivalent check cannot be run for them. Next we examine how abilities and response times depend on age and whether they differ by sex.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rt-angle
#| fig-cap: "**Response time by angle within age groups and site.** Filled points with error bars and dotted lines reflect descriptive cell means and their 95% CIs; solid lines reflect model fits, with grey ribbons for their 95% CIs; color indicates stimulus type. The small translucent dots behind them are individual trials, with RTs outside of ±2 SDs from the mean not shown for visualization clarity. Age bands are shown for visualization only, as age was modeled as a continuous predictor."
#| fig-align: "center"
#| include: true
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 9

# RT axis breaks and labels
rt_labels <- c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8)
rt_breaks <- log(rt_labels)

# panel labellers
age_labeller <- \(x) if_else(x == "", "", glue("Age (years): {x}"))
dataset_labeller <- \(x) if_else(x == "", "", glue("Site: {x}"))

ggplot(avg_preds, aes(x = angle_level)) +
  facet_grid(vars(site_label), vars(age_group),
             labeller = labeller(.cols = age_labeller, .rows = dataset_labeller)) +
  # fake points to make discrete x axis work
  geom_point(aes(y = -Inf), colour = "white", alpha = 0,
             data = tibble(angle_level = fct_inorder(levels(angle_levels$angle_level)))) +
  # observations
  geom_sina(aes(y = log_rt, colour = stimulus),
            data = mrot_lme_data_plot, position = position_identity(),
            size = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, seed = 3141) +
  # model fit CI
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, group = stimulus),
              fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  # empirical mean + CI
  geom_pointrange(aes(y = mean_rt, ymin = ci_lower, ymax = ci_upper, colour = stimulus),
                  linewidth = 0.5, size = 0.1, data = rt_summary) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean_rt, group = stimulus, colour = stimulus),
            linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", data = rt_summary) +
  # model fit
  geom_line(aes(y = estimate, group = stimulus, colour = stimulus)) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = angle_levels$angle_level) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = rt_breaks, labels = rt_labels) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set2",
                      breaks = c("duck", "rabbit", "shape"),
                      labels = c("2D (duck)", "2D (rabbit)", "3D")) +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (°)", y = "Response time (seconds, log scale)",
       colour = "Stimulus type") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-slopes
#| tbl-cap: "**Angle slope marginal effects.** Angle slope represents the difference in log response time per unit of angle (40°). For each predictor, estimates are shown for each of its values (e.g. 2D and 3D items) and for the pairwise differences between its values (e.g. 3D - 2D). Interpretation converts the effects from log space (additive) to response time in seconds (multiplicative), with (ns) indicating that the effect is not statistically significant at $\\alpha$ = .05. Two contrasts are given for stimulus type. The full-range contrast compares each type over the angles it was actually administered, and is not like-for-like, because only 2D items were presented at 160° and that segment is the steepest. The 40--120° contrast restricts both types to the angles they share and is the interpretable comparison."

slopes_tbl |>
  mutate(value = map(value, latex)) |>
  gt(groupname_col = "predictor") |>
  tab_header(title = md("")) |>
  cols_label_with(fn = str_to_sentence) |>
  cols_label("value" = "Predictor", "std.error" = "SE", "p.value" = "p-value") |>
  cols_align(align = "left", columns = value)
```

{{< include _03_sex_diffs.qmd >}}

## Demographic differences

<!-- Scalar invariance establishes structural equivalence across sites, but does not on its own confirm that $\theta$ reflects meaningful variation in mental rotation ability. As a check on construct validity, @fig-ability-age shows participants' IRT-estimated ability ($\theta$) against age, with GAM (generalized additive model)-smoothed trends shown as a visualization aid to highlight the general shape of developmental trajectories without imposing a linear form; formal statistical modeling of these trends is reported in @Kachergis2025LEVANTEcoretasks. Across all four sites, ability increases with age, confirming that the task is sensitive to developmental change — a prerequisite for the individual-differences analyses that follow. The dispersion of points within age bands also underscores the substantial individual variability among same-aged children that motivates our strategy analysis. Note that level differences between site trajectories reflect differences in sample composition and should not be interpreted as cross-cultural differences in ability. -->

<!-- Our third research question examined whether sex differences in mental rotation ability are detectable in this sample, and whether any such differences interact with age. -->

### Age and sex differences in ability

A total of `r ability_sex_stats$n_runs` assessments contributed to the analysis (M age = `r ability_sex_stats$age_mean`, SD = `r ability_sex_stats$age_sd`). Sex was not recorded for every child, and coverage varies by site, so this subsample over-represents the two Colombian sites relative to the full sample (Table S10). Averaging the angle model's slope over this subsample rather than over all trials leaves it essentially unchanged, so the compositional difference does not itself bias the estimates reported here.
Our model predicts ability from sex (female, male), age (`r ability_sex_stats$age_min`--`r ability_sex_stats$age_max` years), site (uniandes-co-bogota, uniandes-co-rural, mpieva-de, western-ca), and all of their possible interactions, along with participant-level random intercepts.
This model's conditional $r^2$ was `r ability_sex_mod_tbl$R2_conditional`, its marginal $r^2$ was `r ability_sex_mod_tbl$R2_marginal`, and its RMSE is `r ability_sex_mod_tbl$RMSE` units of ability. @fig-sex-plot (A) shows the resulting model fits and individual observations.

We found that abilities increased with age (`{r} slope_str(ability_sex_comp("age", "+1"))`), corresponding to an increase of `{r} round(ability_sex_comp("age", "+1")$estimate_sd, 2)` standard deviations of ability per year. Ability is on the latent $\theta$ scale, whose standard deviation in this sample is `{r} round(sd_ability, 2)` rather than 1, because the scalar invariance model estimates each site's ability variance freely relative to a reference site. We found no difference in ability by sex (`{r} slope_str(ability_sex_comp("sex", "Male - Female"))`) and no difference in age slope by sex (`{r} slope_diff_str(ability_slope_diffs)`). Expressed in standard deviations of ability, the sex difference is `{r} sprintf("%.2f", ability_sex_ci$estimate)` SD with a 95% confidence interval of [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", ability_sex_ci$conf.low)`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", ability_sex_ci$conf.high)`], so the data are inconsistent with a difference larger than about `{r} sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(c(ability_sex_ci$conf.low, ability_sex_ci$conf.high))))` SD in either direction. This bound excludes the male advantage of g $\approx$ 0.20 that @lauer2019development report as emerging from around age 6.

The null also held within each site, rather than only on average (@tbl-sex-by-site), and adding the sex-by-site interaction did not improve model fit ($\chi^2$(`{r} ability_sex_site_lrt$df`) = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", ability_sex_site_lrt$chisq)`, *p* `{r} fmt_p(ability_sex_site_lrt$p.value)`). The largest site-level estimate was at western-ca, where the point estimate favoured girls, but the sample there is the smallest and the interval is correspondingly wide.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sex-by-site
#| tbl-cap: "**Sex differences in mental rotation ability within each site.** Estimates are male minus female, expressed in standard deviations of ability, with 95% confidence intervals. Negative values favour girls."

ability_sex_by_site |>
  mutate(ci = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", conf.low, conf.high),
         estimate = sprintf("%+.2f", estimate)) |>
  select(site_label, estimate, ci, p.value) |>
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Site", "Estimate (SD)", "95% CI", "p-value"),
    booktabs = TRUE, linesep = "", align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
  )
```

### Sex differences in response time

We do not report a direct comparison of mean response time levels by age, since these conflate developmental change with differences in the items children were administered (older children saw a higher proportion of 3D trials, for which response times are longer). Age is instead examined through its effect on the angle slope, reported above. As such, we examine angle sensitivity using the model described above, but with the addition of a sex predictor.

A total of `r rt_sex_stats$n_runs` assessments contributed `r rt_sex_stats$n_trials` trials to the analysis (M age = `r rt_sex_stats$age_mean`, SD = `r rt_sex_stats$age_sd`).
Our model predicts response time (in log transformed seconds) from angle (20°--160°), stimulus type (2D duck, 2D rabbit, 3D), site (uniandes-co-bogota, uniandes-co-rural, mpieva-de, western-ca), age (`r rt_sex_stats$age_min`--`r rt_sex_stats$age_max` years), sex (female, male), and all of their possible interactions, along with participant-level random intercepts and random slopes of angle.
This model's conditional $r^2$ was `r rt_sex_mod_tbl$R2_conditional`, its marginal $r^2$ was `r rt_sex_mod_tbl$R2_marginal`, and its RMSE is `r rt_sex_mod_tbl$RMSE` on the log scale, equivalent to a multiplicative error of about `r rt_sex_mod_tbl$RMSE_exp`× in response time. @fig-sex-plot (B) shows the resulting model fits and individual observations.

We found a relatively small but robust effect of sex (`{r} slope_str(rt_sex_comp("mrot"))`), corresponding to boys being on average `{r} rt_sex_comp("mrot")$interpretation` than girls. The effect holds for both stimulus types (2D `{r} slope_str(rt_sex_comp("2d"))`, `{r} rt_sex_comp("2d")$interpretation`; 3D `{r} slope_str(rt_sex_comp("3d"))`, `{r} rt_sex_comp("3d")$interpretation`), though it is smaller and less precisely estimated for 3D items, and does not survive a balanced weighting of the design (Table S11). Boys therefore responded somewhat faster without performing better. We find no difference in angle slope, with both girls (`{r} slope_str(rt_sex_slope("Female"))`) and boys (`{r} slope_str(rt_sex_slope("Male"))`) being about `{r} rt_sex_slope("mrot")$interpretation`. We report these comparisons without correction for multiple testing. Because the inference of interest concerns the absence of sex differences, uncorrected tests provide the more stringent standard for that claim.
 
```{r}
#| label: fig-sex-plot
#| fig-cap: "**Mental rotation ability (A) and response time (B) by sex assigned at birth**. Points in A represent assessments while points in B represent individual trials; lines reflect model fits, with grey ribbons for their 95% CIs (2D stimuli as solid lines, 3D stimuli as dashed lines)."
#| include: true
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7.5

# site_n_labels <- mrot_df_sex |>
#   distinct(run_id, site_label) |>
#   count(site_label) |>
#   mutate(label = paste0(site_label, "\n(n = ", n, ")"))

plt_sex_ability <- ggplot(mrot_df_sex, aes(x = age)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(site_label),
             labeller = labeller(.cols = dataset_labeller)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ability, colour = sex), alpha = 0.35, size = 1.1) +
  geom_ribbon(data = ability_sex_preds,
              aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, group = sex),
              fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = ability_sex_preds,
            aes(y = estimate, group = sex, colour = sex)) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.02)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Ability (θ)", colour = "Sex") +
  # guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(fill = NA))) +
  guides(color = "none") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

plt_sex_rt <- ggplot(sex_preds, aes(x = angle_level)) +
  facet_grid(cols = vars(site_label),
             labeller = labeller(.cols = dataset_labeller)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = -Inf), colour = "white", alpha = 0,
             data = tibble(angle_level = fct_inorder(levels(angle_levels$angle_level)))) +
  geom_sina(aes(y = log_rt, colour = sex), data = mrot_lme_data_sex_plot,
            position = position_identity(), #maxwidth = 1,
            size = 0.1, alpha = 0.05, seed = 3141) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high, group = interaction(sex, stimulus)),
              fill = "lightgrey", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line(aes(y = estimate, group = interaction(sex, stimulus),
                colour = sex, linetype = item_group)) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = angle_levels$angle_level) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = rt_breaks, labels = rt_labels) +
  scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_linetype(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (°)", y = "Response time\n(seconds, log scale)",
       colour = "Sex") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

plt_sex_ability + plt_sex_rt +
  plot_layout(ncol = 1) +
  plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```


# Discussion

The central aim of this study was to establish whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task measures the same underlying construct across four culturally diverse sites. The answer, across three distinct levels of analysis, is largely yes. The task achieves measurement invariance at least at the metric level — including across two sites in Colombia, an upper-middle-income country in the Global South — indicating that the ordering of items by difficulty and their capacity to discriminate among children are consistent across cultural contexts [@putnick2016measurement]. The angular disparity effect replicates for both 2D and 3D stimuli across all four sites, providing process-level evidence that performance is driven by the spatial demands of the task in the way theory predicts [@shepard1971mental] — a form of evidence that is distinct from, and complementary to, the psychometric result. Among the youngest children at the two Colombian sites the effect is not detectable in the unrestricted data, but it emerges clearly once children responding at chance are excluded, so this reflects performance near the guessing floor rather than a site where the task fails to engage mental rotation. The absence of a main effect of sex or any age-by-sex interaction is consistent with the meta-analytic picture for child-friendly tasks in this age range [@lauer2019development], and its replication across all four international sites extends prior null findings beyond the Western convenience samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. That these convergent forms of evidence emerge across geographically and culturally diverse samples supports the interpretation that the task is capturing individual differences in a common spatial reasoning construct rather than one that is specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was developed.

## Cross-site invariance
Turning to our first research question, the invariance analyses establish that the mental rotation task functions comparably across pilot sites. Items have the same ordering by difficulty and discriminate similarly for children in Bogotá, Leipzig, and London, Ontario, and ability estimates can be placed on a common latent scale [@putnick2016measurement]. The configural model, in which every item parameter is free to differ by site, is decisively rejected under every prior specification we examined. Whether the stricter scalar constraint on item difficulties also holds is less clear, since that comparison is sensitive to the strength of the prior placed on item discriminations (Table S1), and we therefore do not rest anything on it. The demographic results reported above are unchanged when ability is estimated under the metric model instead. This finding is notable because tasks developed in one context do not automatically achieve psychometric equivalence when administered elsewhere [@van2004bias], and the inclusion of two sites in Colombia, an upper-middle-income country in the Global South makes this a stronger test than studies conducted entirely within high-income North American and European samples. That said, scalar invariance establishes metric comparability rather than cultural equivalence in any deeper sense. With only one non-Western country represented — though through two sites spanning both urban and rural schools, representing a meaningfully different cultural and socioeconomic context from the German and Canadian samples — the present findings should be treated as an encouraging foundation rather than evidence of broad cross-cultural portability. Further validation across more culturally and socioeconomically diverse sites will be needed before stronger claims can be made. The LEVANTE network has since expanded to include sites in Ghana, India, Peru and Argentina, and further communities in Colombia, as well as additional high-income samples across North America, Europe and Australia. This will provide the opportunity to subject these findings to a more demanding cross-cultural test. Finally, given that LEVANTE sites differ substantially in sampling, recruitment, and testing format, site-level performance differences are not interpreted here regardless of the invariance results; however, we believe the consistency of patterns within and across sites remains informative.

## Angular sensitivity
Our second research question asked whether performance is driven by the spatial properties of the stimuli. The key benchmark here is the angular disparity effect first reported by @shepard1971mental: as the rotational distance between a target and its match increases, so too does the time required to judge whether they correspond. This relationship, among the most replicated findings in cognitive psychology [@cooper1973chronometric; @peters2008applications], has been demonstrated extensively in children and adults from middle-to-high-income Western convenience samples [@kaltner2016developmental; @jansen2015role]. The present study examines whether this relationship extends across the culturally diverse child samples represented in the pilot sites. Its emergence here in every site, and in every age band among children performing above chance (Table S8), suggests that the underlying cognitive process it indexes — the spatially continuous transformation of object orientation — is not specific to the cultural or educational contexts in which it was originally documented. Our models estimate a multiplicative rather than an additive angle effect: response times were modelled on a log scale, so the reported slopes describe a constant percentage increase per 40° rather than the constant per-degree increment implied by a fixed rotation rate. What replicates here is therefore the monotonic dependence of response time on angular disparity rather than the strictly linear chronometric function reported in adults. This finding adds a distinct form of evidence beyond psychometric equivalence by addressing process-level validity. It is one thing to show that a task achieves comparable difficulty ordering across sites; it is another to show that performance is sensitive to the spatial structure of the stimuli in the way that mental rotation theory predicts [@borsboom2004concept]. The angular disparity effect provides the latter, and its cross-cultural replication substantially strengthens the case that the task is engaging spatial cognition specifically, rather than some culturally-variable combination of task-general skills. Response times were substantially longer for 3D than for 2D stimuli throughout, consistent with the greater difficulty of the 3D geometric figures relative to the familiar duck and rabbit silhouettes [@folk1987effects; @bethell1988mental]. The angular disparity effect is present for both stimulus types under any weighting of the data, but its magnitude for the 3D items is less precisely determined than for the 2D items, because 3D trials are concentrated in the older children and over a narrower range of angles.

Children at mpieva-de showed both higher baseline response times and steeper RT–angle slopes than the other three sites. Remote home-based testing on family devices, as used at mpieva-de, may introduce environmental variability that inflates both baseline RT and trial-to-trial noise [@backx2020comparing], and because absolute slopes scale with baseline speed, slower responding will mechanically enlarge an absolute slope. That mechanism accounts for part of the difference but not all of it. Because the multiplicative slopes reported here are already expressed relative to each site's own baseline, mpieva-de's position as the steepest site on this scale cannot be explained by slower responding alone, and it remains reliably steeper than each of the other three sites (@tbl-slopes). Some genuine difference in angular sensitivity therefore remains, although the confounding of site with testing format means we cannot confidently attribute it to either. Per-run raw response time distributions are shown in Figure S5.

## Demographic differences

Our analyses also speak to how mental rotation changes with age. Ability increased steadily across the 5--13 year range, consistent with the prolonged developmental trajectory documented for this skill [@frick2013development; @marmor1975development; @kail1980developmental]. The angular disparity effect also steepened with age, with the multiplicative cost of each additional 40° of rotation smallest in the youngest children and largest in the oldest. This steepening is not an artifact of the logarithmic scale. Older children responded faster overall, which would if anything inflate a multiplicative slope for a given absolute cost, yet their absolute cost per additional 40° was also the largest, and the same ordering by age holds when response times are measured in seconds rather than log units (Table S5). Part of the gradient is nonetheless attributable to how accurately children were performing rather than to development as such. Angle slopes are strongly related to accuracy, and because accuracy rises with age, the youngest children contribute the flattest slopes. Restricting the analysis to assessments completed well above chance roughly halves the age gradient, from 0.11 to 0.06 log units per 40° (Table S7). We are cautious about the mechanism. Chance responding is the obvious candidate, since a child answering at random still produces correct trials whose response times carry no information about angular disparity, but it does not account for the pattern on its own. Among assessments below 60% accuracy the angle slope is reliably negative rather than merely flat (-0.06, SE = 0.02), and random responding can only attenuate a slope toward zero, not reverse it. Responding faster to items that appear harder points to disengagement alongside guessing. What the data establish is that a substantial share of the apparent developmental change reflects near-chance performance, not which of these processes produces it.

A smaller gradient survives that restriction at every threshold we examined, however, and accuracy and age band each predict the slope when both are entered together. The remainder is consistent with a developmental shift in how the task is solved. Younger children's response times depend comparatively little on angular disparity, as would be expected if they rely more often on strategies that are insensitive to rotation -- matching local features, responding before a transformation is complete, or abandoning the attempt. Those strategies are also what low accuracy indexes, so the measurement account and the developmental one are less distinct than they first appear. On this reading the steeper slope in older children is not a loss of efficiency but a signature of continuous mental rotation becoming the dominant approach.

Our third research question asked whether sex differences in mental rotation ability are detectable in this sample, and whether any such differences interact with age. The absence of a main effect of sex or an age-by-sex interaction replicates the pattern reported in several recent studies of primary school-aged children using child-friendly mental rotation tasks [@hodgkiss2021developmental; @lauer2019development], and is consistent with the meta-analytic picture, in which reliable sex differences in mental rotation are small and inconsistent in this age range, particularly for tasks using 2D stimuli and child-friendly formats of the kind used here [@lauer2019development]. Notably, the null finding held within each of the four international study sites and not merely on average, extending prior null results beyond the middle-to-high-income Western samples in which they have predominantly been documented [@hodgkiss2021developmental]. The interval on the overall effect also rules out a difference of the magnitude reported meta-analytically for children from around age 6 onward [@lauer2019development], so this is an informative null rather than simply an underpowered one. These null results concern mental rotation ability. Response times did differ, with boys responding somewhat faster than girls. Because boys were no more accurate, a speed difference of this kind is not evidence of a spatial advantage and may instead reflect response style or a speed--accuracy tradeoff. Taken together, the sex difference results are consistent with the broader argument of this paper: that the task captures a spatially-driven construct that is consistent across cultural contexts.


## Limitations
Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. Although the four sites span three countries and different linguistic contexts, two of the three partner teams collected data in middle-to-high-income Western settings, and while the Colombian site is more socioeconomically diverse — spanning urban schools in Bogotá and rural schools in surrounding departments — the sample as a whole remains far from representative of the full range of cultural environments in which children develop. The LEVANTE project has already expanded substantially since this initial data collection, including new sites in low- and middle-income countries, which will broaden the cultural scope of findings like those reported here. Sample sizes were also unbalanced across sites, with the Canadian sample smaller overall, which limits the precision of site-level estimates and the power to detect cross-site differences. The two stimulus types were administered over different angle ranges, with 3D items presented only between 40° and 120°, so comparisons of angular sensitivity between stimulus types are restricted to the angles both types received. 3D items were also administered disproportionately to older children, who show steeper angle slopes, so the 3D estimate is more sensitive than the 2D estimate to how trials are weighted (`r sprintf("%.2f", obs_item_slopes[["3d"]])` averaging over the observed trials against `r sprintf("%.2f", grid_item_slopes[["3d"]])` weighting age bands equally; Table S4). The magnitude of the 3D effect is therefore less firmly established than its presence. The sex analyses rest on the subset of assessments for which sex was recorded, and because coverage of that variable differs across sites, the subsample is not composed like the full sample. The angle slope is unaffected by this, but the sex comparisons themselves cannot be checked against the children for whom sex is missing, so their generalisation to the full sample rests on an assumption we are unable to test. The cross-sectional design is a further constraint, in that developmental trajectories here are inferred from age differences between children rather than observed directly. Longitudinal data are currently being collected and processed, however, and will allow this question to be addressed more directly in due course. 

# Conclusion
Three research questions motivated this study, each asking in a different way whether the LEVANTE mental rotation task is doing consistent and interpretable work across culturally diverse settings. Across all three, the answer is largely affirmative. Measurement invariance holds across sites, at least at the metric level, including two sites in Colombia, an upper-middle-income country in the Global South; the angular disparity effect replicates as a process-level signature of spatial engagement; and sex differences are absent in a pattern consistent with the meta-analytic picture for this age range and task types. These findings do not mean that mental rotation development is uniform across children or contexts — the substantial individual variability within sites suggests there is much still to understand about what drives variation in spatial ability across children. But they do mean that the task is measuring something consistent — that when a child in Bogotá, a child in Leipzig, and a child in London (Ontario) sit down to judge whether two rotated objects are the same, they are, by and large, making use of the same general set of spatial abilities. Such consistency is the foundation on which meaningful cross-cultural comparisons can be built.
